title: Sameer Samat on Android 17 and the Future of Intelligent Computing
description: Sameer Samat, President of Android at Google, joins host Logan Kilpatrick to discuss Android 17 and what it means to shift from operating systems to intelligence systems. Their conversation covers why Android didn't say the word AI once at the Android Show, the new Gemini Intelligence feature suite including Rambler, app automation, Superfill, and generative widgets, and what it looks like when Gemini can see the road with you in a live demo inside a Volvo EX60.

segments.heading: Why the Android Show never used the word AI
segments.text:
Logan Kilpatrick opens on the difficulty of the job the Android team has: bringing this technology to literally billions of people. He notes that Sameer Samat did not say the word AI once during the Android Show, and that the ecosystem is currently focused on the technology rather than on what it does for the real people using the devices.

Samat frames it as knowing your audience. The Android Show audience is largely people using devices who are excited about technology and want the product they already use to get better. Some are deep on AI, but many are not, because it is a much wider audience. Something is going on with the word AI itself: there is a reaction to it, it is scary for some people, it means different things to different people, and it has become overloaded. Inside Google, and among technologists generally, it is understood as a huge moment and a platform shift that changes everything. But from a consumer standpoint the lesson they have learned is not to lead with the tech, and instead to lead with the benefit.

The feature that taught them this was Circle to Search, launched a couple of years earlier. The concept is simple: hold down the Home button on an Android phone, the screen lights up, and you can circle any object on the screen. It might be the tie someone is wearing that you are interested in, or the lake in a photo on a social media post. Then you ask a question about it: where do I buy that, how do I get there, what is that thing. It worked because these things were genuinely hard to describe to Google before. Samat's point is that if you could describe the tie or the lake well enough to search for it, you would probably already know what it was.

The feature took off. There is a great deal of AI and machine vision behind it, but none of that was mentioned in how it was presented. They showed what you could do with it and people loved it. On other features where they led with the AI, the reception was cooler: people responded with a version of "I don't know about your AI, I'm not feeling that as much." So the show used the word AI zero times even though a lot of the features in it are AI powered, and Samat believes the reception was better that way, because people were being told why something is good and helpful in their life.

segments.heading: Leading with the benefit: on-device scam detection built with DeepMind
segments.text:
Kilpatrick raises the tension in how much AI to lead with, given that everyone is asking who to bet on during a platform shift. His own read is that Android is at the absolute frontier of pushing that shift forward, and he asks how it has actually shown up in the product.

Samat's answer is that the technology matters because it helps build better experiences for the user, and that is fundamentally what drives the team. What the models can do is genuinely wild. There are things Android wanted to do for a long time and could not. He describes seeing mockups of a new feature or concept from a product manager who had not been around long, and having to say that it was not going to work. Now his response is to bring all of those back, because he thinks the tech is ready for them.

His concrete example is scam and spam protection. Android is very popular in a number of countries where the rate of scam and spam is high, which means a lot of phone calls and text messages trying to get you to part with information you should not share. Working with Google DeepMind, they built an on-device model that, with the user's permission, can listen to a call from an unknown number. They worked with a number of banks to make sure the model understood what a bank would never ask a customer for. Banks have consortiums and associations where they agree on those rules together. If the model hears one of those prohibited requests during the call, a warning pops up and the phone vibrates to say that this is a scam and you should hang up right now.

Samat considers that the promise of the technology, and something that affects a very large number of people positively. It is a big part of Android's strategy, but the way to describe it to people is in terms of what it does for you. Kilpatrick adds that Demis Hassabis makes the same point in these planning conversations: technology that works for you. The tension is that Google also wants to say it is at the lead and at the frontier, and those two messages pull against each other.

segments.heading: Balancing on-device models across flagship and entry-level devices
segments.text:
Kilpatrick notes that the scam detection model runs on device, and that a set of recent events made on-device models legible to a lot of people at once: the OpenClaw moment, the release of Gemma 4, and people downloading the AI Edge Gallery app and experimenting with it. Many people suddenly understood that on-device models are going to be powerful and capable and will enable new experiences.

He frames Android's specific tension: there are billions of devices, running the models requires high-end new hardware because it is more performant, and there is a whole group of people without high-end devices who would benefit from AI the most. He asks what the open and on-device model strategy looks like from a platform perspective.

Samat agrees the on-device model strategy is evolving right now, because on-device models are becoming seriously impressive and he thinks they are on the cusp of something amazing. Android's mission is to bring the best of computing to everyone in the world: that means high-end devices and the most basic device you can buy.

He describes two distinct innovation motions. The first is at the high end, creating the future using flagship devices, because those have more system resources. Before you know how to optimize, you use all the system resources available and push the boundary of what is possible. The second motion is flowing those capabilities down, which requires a different approach: you take the kernel of what was built at the flagship level, identify the features that are most profound and most interesting, and find ways to run them on less capable devices. Sometimes that means using the server. Sometimes it means creating different specialized on-device models, and working with silicon providers so those models run efficiently within thermal and battery constraints.

Samat says Android has done this effectively over the years and describes the pattern as sinusoidal. Right now the focus is on the flagship side because that is where the innovation is happening. Some features, including scam detection, are already on device and working for people. The next phase is flowing them down over time.

segments.heading: From operating systems to intelligence systems
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks what the symbiosis between new models and newly unlocked capabilities means at a macro level for Android, and whether the experience five years out, when models are good enough to run well on the hardware most people already own, will be a totally different experience.

Samat takes a step back to frame it. For the last forty-plus years, computing has created systems that put the user in the role of micromanager of the system. First there was a command line interface asking what you would like to do. Then came the graphical user interface with menus and pointing devices. But it is still the user who conceptualizes the goal, breaks that goal down into all the discrete actions required, and then literally clicks through the sub-actions one at a time. That is the micromanager model of computing, and it remains intimidating: people still take classes to learn software.

The opportunity, and how Samat describes the next several years of Android, is to go from operating systems to intelligence systems. In an intelligence system the user articulates goals, and the system's job is managing resources, managing context, and figuring out how to turn those goals plus the surrounding context into the actions the user wants. Android plans to get this right on flagship devices first. Over time he expects the interface itself to change and become more intent-to-action oriented rather than micromanagement oriented.

segments.heading: Rambler: rebuilding the keyboard around voice, with a live demo
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks how this changes in the shorter term, and how much voice, which has taken off as a new interface, shows up in the new experiences.

Samat notes that people tend to jump straight to agents when he talks about intent to action, and that agents matter, but he is glad voice came up because input method is one of the fundamental parts of an operating system: how does the user tell the system what they want done. A big part of that is the keyboard, whether on the phone or physical, and it has not changed much in a long time. The last big addition was autocomplete, which he dates to roughly 2012, or possibly 2013 or 2014. Swipe was another addition. Kilpatrick notes he is still fighting autocomplete daily, and Samat agrees it could be a lot better.

Samat calls the keyboard the perfect example of a micromanagement input system: you think about what you want to say, work out the goal of what you are trying to say, break it into the specific words you want to use, and then peck out the letters of those words. It is so habitual that nobody thinks about it.

The feature they announced to change this is called Rambler, rolling out in summer 2026. When you tap the microphone you simply ramble. Instead of faithfully transcribing exactly what you said in dictation form, Rambler takes everything you said and distills it down to what you actually wanted to say, shows it to you for confirmation, and then you send it. Samat connects this to an existing human habit: giving someone a brain dump of your ideas is productive, because verbalizing surfaces things, and the other person reflects back what was interesting. Rambler is the machine equivalent.

The live demo runs inside Google Messages, using the microphone in Google Keyboard, which Samat notes is used hundreds of millions of times a day for voice dictation. He rambles: "Hey there, if you're going to the store, can you pick up some fruit? Maybe like some bananas, mangoes, strawberries, and oranges. Actually, never mind the bananas. We don't need any more of those. We have plenty of those." The result contains none of the hesitation sounds, and the self-correction about bananas is resolved rather than transcribed: the model understands the bananas are not wanted. He then asks it to turn the text into a list and to add some emoji, and it does both.

Kilpatrick asks whether it runs on device. Samat says no, this is currently talking to the server, and they have made it very fast. A deliberate tuning decision: they did not want the output to read in a style people associate with a chatbot, so it is tuned for a more conversational tone. That is why it did not produce a list initially and had to be asked. Samat calls the added emoji gratuitous but did it anyway.

Rambler works for simple texts and equally well for dictating something longer like a paper. It will be a mode you can use the microphone in, and typing on the keyboard remains available. Samat presents it as a major upgrade to the keyboard and a large part of what they mean by an intelligent system: the keyboard itself is now intelligent.

segments.heading: App Automation and Android's virtual window system
segments.text:
Kilpatrick frames input as the first step of the transformation and actions taken on the device as the second: Android going and clicking things in the phone, so the user articulates intent in voice and Android does the micromanaging.

Samat confirms this is the feature they call App Automation, and it is exactly what it sounds like: you tell Gemini you want to get something done. Kilpatrick points out that App Automation is the ideal illustration of the naming principle, because the name sells the outcome, automating apps on your phone, rather than the AI.

When shown to people, the reaction is a mix of being impressed and being a little nervous, so the team worked to make it approachable. The main mechanism is a virtual window system built into Android.

Samat grounds it in his preferred example, chosen because it has real complexity. He has a list of people coming to his barbecue on screen, and each person in the list has the size of their party and whether they are vegetarian. He long-presses the power button, which brings up screen context for Gemini so it can see the document with him, and asks Gemini to go to Instacart and put what he will need for the barbecue for all these people into his cart at Safeway.

When Gemini starts Automation, it opens the task in a virtual window: a containerized environment where the designated app and Gemini both exist, and which the user can minimize into the status bar and return to at any time. The AI agent cannot go outside that container, which means it cannot use other apps. The user can watch it work, and Samat says it is sometimes fun to watch, because the model's thinking appears at the bottom of the screen as it goes.

In his run of the barbecue example, the agent navigated through Safeway and independently arrived at the observation that hot dog buns and hot dogs never come in matching package counts. Its visible reasoning worked through needing more buns than hot dogs and how to resolve that. It also worked out that veggie burgers were needed, added everything to the cart, and then sent a notification saying the cart was ready for review.

A deliberate safety boundary: Automation stops before completing transactions. Samat says building trust with the consumer and having that safety around it matters right now, so the agent hands back and the user pushes the commit button themselves. The time saving is the proposition.

Kilpatrick asks whether containerized apps running on the phone existed before. Samat says Android has always had an app container and a per-app isolation layer, but the notion of something else driving the screen while confined to that container, inside a minimizable virtual window, is new. There was no need for it before, because these are single-user systems where the user is on the device doing their own thing, and a headless process generating UI in the background served no purpose. The model does need it, because it has to look at and see what is on the screen.

On the longer term, Samat sees three approaches converging under the agent: MCP integrations, Chrome doing a form of auto browse to manage and complete things, and this screen-driving approach. The user tells Gemini what they want done and Gemini decides which of these tools is best.

Asked whether Automation is vision-based, Samat confirms it is: Gemini looks at the screen and chooses coordinates to tap, using the app just as a person would. It decides to open a menu, opens it, taps the search bar, and starts searching for hot dog buns. The intended user model is handing your phone to a trusted assistant and asking them to get something done for you.

segments.heading: Gemini Intelligence and Superfill: never fill out a form again
segments.text:
Kilpatrick asks about Gemini Intelligence, which is what kicks off the Automation workflow, for anyone who missed the headline.

Samat explains they wanted a way to describe the best Gemini experience, and Gemini Intelligence is that name. It was announced at the Android Show a couple of weeks before this conversation, and it covers a set of capabilities at the bleeding edge. Rambler and Automation are part of it.

The capability he is most enthusiastic about is Superfill. His motivation is personal and blunt: he wants to get rid of forms and never fill one out again. After booking a set of flights for a summer vacation he has his fifteen-year-old's passport number memorized, which he does not want to have memorized. Kilpatrick notes he does not even know his own passport number.

Superfill extends a familiar idea. Autofill already works for your name, your address, and possibly your credit card information. Superfill is that, extended to many other fields. If you have given Gemini permission, which Samat stresses is an important step, it can pull information that already exists in your Google account and suggest it in real time as you fill out a form: a passport uploaded to Google Photos, a confirmation code sitting in an email.

Kilpatrick asks about the mechanism. Does the model notice an open form field and try to retrieve something plausible, or is there a fixed set of categories it pulls into personal context? Samat says that initially, to get the precision and recall trade-off right and to make sure users become comfortable enough to rely on it, they have limited it to a set of entity types: passport information, driver's licenses, and vehicle license plates.

His favorite case is the license plate. The DMV registration is sitting in your email. You park somewhere, scan the QR code in the parking lot, and the parking app asks for your car's license plate while you are already walking out of the lot, which normally sends you searching through Photos or Gmail. With Superfill it is offered to you directly.

The implementation: a system has already retrieved those entities and holds them pre-prepared in a centralized repository. When the on-device system detects that you are looking at a form needing one of those entities, it makes a secure request to pull that information and presents it in the keyboard, asking whether you want to autofill it. If you accept, it grabs the value and puts it in the field. Samat says all of this is coming in summer 2026.

As an aside, Kilpatrick lobbies for renaming Rambler to something built on the word Yap, suggesting Yap Mode, on the grounds that people love to yap. Samat says it is a good point and he would have to check whether it is trademarkable.

segments.heading: Generative widgets and the beginning of generative UI in the OS
segments.text:
The last Gemini Intelligence capability Samat covers is generative widgets, which he thinks speaks to how UI may evolve.

Widgets are the ultimate form of customization on Android and have long been a loved way to customize the home screen, but someone has to build the widget for you first. The generative widget concept removes that dependency: you tell Gemini what you want to see, for example the latest lap times for yesterday's F1 race, and ask it to keep that updated and build you the widget. Nobody may have built that particular widget. Gemini works on it for a while and produces exactly that widget, pulling from publicly available sources of information.

Samat calls this the beginning of generative UI for your operating system, and expects the pattern to expand over time so that more of the UI is built for you on the fly.

segments.heading: Does the agentic shift kill apps: experiential versus transactional
segments.text:
Kilpatrick recalls the line that Android is the platform for builders, and notes everything discussed so far delivers on it. He then raises a question he likes to ask inside Google: will Google in five years have ten thousand products or three products, ten thousand apps or three apps. His point is that Android, as an operating system whose predominant interface is showing up and going through apps, faces interesting implications. More people are building apps than ever before, while at the same time everyone appears to be trying to build super apps.

Samat calls it a genuinely interesting moment, because there is talk that there will be no reason for apps at the same time as a wave of first-time developers is being created.

He does not think apps go away. He relates it to what people call the SaaS-pocalypse, where SaaS companies were hit hard on the theory that agentic AI removes the need for those applications: users will either make their own or the existing products lose their UIs and become commoditized backends. Samat considers that a surface-deep way of looking at what will actually happen, because not all SaaS is the same. Applying the same shallow reasoning to what he calls the app-pocalypse requires going deeper.

Part of going deeper is understanding consumer behavior. Looking at what consumers actually do on their phones, they spend seventy to eighty plus percent of their time in apps he would call experiential: TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, chatting with friends, playing games. That is the bulk of time spent. Apps that are more transactional in nature, such as booking a ride or getting a meal, account for some of the time, but less than you would expect. Less time spent does not mean less important.

He suggests plotting apps on a two-by-two, one axis being how experiential an app is and the other how transactional, since apps can sit in the middle. Time clusters on the experiential, less transactional side.

From this he concludes the grid of apps will evolve, but he does not think anyone wants their agent watching TikTok or YouTube for them. Users still want to kick back and do some of that themselves, engage with friends on messaging, and play their games. The transactional apps are the ones that will change most, and he expects those to end up with two modes: an experiential version offering a much richer, more engaging experience, and a mode where the app is almost agentic itself, responding to agentic queries from others.

His example is Google Maps, with the caveat that he does not run the Maps team. Maps has an Ask Maps feature, which he reads as its agentic mode of being. Planning an event, you might ask your agent for great venues around Tahoe. Then, wanting to understand the indoor to outdoor flow of a specific venue, you open Maps yourself, switch to satellite view, zoom in and look around. That second part is the experiential view.

So his conclusion is not that apps go away, but that the transactional side becomes much more nuanced, and that people may end up with more time for experiential apps rather than less.

Kilpatrick draws a parallel to commerce and retail malls, where both ends of the spectrum exist. Buying his mother something at Williams-Sonoma, the staff greeted him warmly and offered him a coffee when he had come in for a spatula, which struck him as deliberately experiential and unlike a normal shopping trip. At the other end, on any of those companies' websites, he is in transaction mode: find the thing, click the fewest buttons, buy it, and leave. Retailers have innovated and changed the way shopping works in store precisely because customers can now transact elsewhere.

Samat adds that easier completion tends to expand overall usage: if something becomes much easier for him to get done, he does more of it. Retail and commerce combined, offline plus online, is larger than it was before. He notes that in every platform shift there is a narrative that the old thing completely goes away, and it usually does not: these things tend to build on each other. The web did not eliminate going to physical locations, and physical experiences are arguably becoming more important. Mobile did not eliminate the desktop. He considers the agentic move huge and profound and does not want to predict that it will not be different, but his expectation is accumulation rather than replacement.

segments.heading: Android Halo: a place in the status bar for long-running agents
segments.text:
The way Android is handling background agent work is a new concept called Android Halo. It is a dedicated location in the status bar where the user's agent of choice, Gemini or another agent, can post updates and take input on the task or tasks it is running.

The reasoning is that an agent doing work in the background will need to ask the user a question, give an update, or show a result, and the user needs somewhere to follow along. Samat presents Halo as an interesting new spot for how computing may evolve, with the operating system making it more seamless to engage with long-running tasks.

segments.heading: Voice as a native interface across form factors
segments.text:
Before moving to the car demo, Kilpatrick asks about text and voice as interfaces from an Android ecosystem perspective, given that voice is one of the native form factors everyone is used to and text is already how people communicate with each other.

Samat says voice is very natural for a lot of people, and in certain form factors it is the only sensible interface: in the car, with a pair of glasses, or on a run with a watch. In those cases it is genuinely valuable that the machine can now understand natural language, because voice was the only available channel and previously the experience was workable but awkward.

He sees a generational shift. Younger consumers, including his own children, hardly type on their phones at all and constantly use the microphone to speak. Sending voice recordings rather than text is common. Voice is also more efficient: you can typically speak three to five times faster than you can type. His conclusion is that embracing voice, with simple and straightforward ways of using it, unlocks new use cases now that the machine understands you much better.

Kilpatrick notes that places where you previously could not wield intelligence are opening up. You could not do anything useful in a car because you had to focus on driving, and that is changing.

segments.heading: Gemini built into the Volvo EX60: natural language car controls
segments.text:
The demo moves into a Volvo EX60, a vehicle that had not shipped at the time of recording.

The car has Google built-in, meaning Google and Gemini run on the infotainment system powered by Android. Because of that, Android and Gemini have much deeper access to the car's systems.

Samat demonstrates climate control by voice: he says the car is stuffy and asks Gemini to adjust the climate. Gemini responds that it is increasing the fan speed and turning off air recirculation, and makes both adjustments. He points out that he would not normally have the climate menu open while driving, so seeing the changes applied on screen is the confirmation.

The second demonstration is a driver assistance control. Without touching any physical controls he asks Gemini to turn on lane keeping assist, and it confirms that it is turning on the lane keeping aid. Samat highlights the speed and the fact that he can speak in natural language: there is no longer a requirement to say an exact phrase in an exact way, which he attributes to Gemini.

segments.heading: Gemini seeing the road with you: front camera grounding
segments.text:
The second capability wired into this vehicle connects Gemini to the car's front-facing cameras. The intent was to find out what becomes possible if Gemini, with the user's permission, can see the world as you drive through it.

Samat is explicit about the privacy design. Gemini is not watching what you are seeing at all times. The camera feed is provided to Gemini only when you invoke it and ask a question, for a limited period. Gemini answers, and then loses the ability to see again. Asked whether it only sees from the moment of activation onward, Samat says it keeps a local buffer.

Three live queries follow. Asked what it sees around them, Gemini reports that they are at the Googleplex in Mountain View surrounded by lush greenery and modern office buildings, and identifies Google Building 1020 Charleston Road on the left, describing its brick-accented exterior and noting it is part of the extensive Landings office complex.

Driving on, Samat asks about a white sculpture ahead on the right and the building behind it, something he says he had always wondered about and could not describe well enough to look up. Gemini identifies the sculpture as the Orb, a thirty-three-foot-tall public art installation made of over 6,400 aluminum panels that create unique light patterns, and the building behind it as Gradient Canopy, noting its signature dragon-scale solar roof that generates a significant portion of the building's own power. Neither host nor guest knew about the solar roof.

The third query asks about a white tent-like set of buildings on the left. Gemini identifies them as part of the Shoreline Amphitheater, an outdoor music venue known for its distinctive peaked roof design, built on a former landfill, now hosting major concerts and festivals in a scenic park-like setting.

Samat frames the open question as how Gemini seeing along with you can genuinely make life easier, and says the team is still working through how best to launch this in vehicles. Kilpatrick suggests grounding against Street View when you are trying to find the right place to turn and the location looks unfamiliar. Samat adds street signs in a different language, or signs that are simply confusing, as cases where explanation on the spot would help.
